turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: And I daresay, 149 Belgrave Square is not the most desirable address, even if it were your own, Mr. Worthing.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't see how my address is relevant to our marriage, Lady Bracknell.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that I am beginning to suspect that your social position is even more dubious than I initially thought.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I hope I may have given you the wrong impression, Lady Bracknell. I assure you that my family's circumstances are quite respectable, even if our address may not be the most fashionable.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist on seeing the family's estate, Mr. Worthing, to verify these claims of respectability. It is simply not acceptable to have a young woman of Gwendolen's standing attached to a man of unknown and possibly questionable background.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand your concerns, Lady Bracknell, and I assure you that my family's estate is quite modest, but perfectly respectable, I assure you.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must admit, Mr. Worthing, that I am growing increasingly skeptical of your assertions. If your family's estate is indeed 'modest' and 'respectable', I should think it would be easy to procure a solicitor's letter to verify this.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I must admit, Lady Bracknell, that I did try to procure a solicitor's letter, but unfortunately, my solicitor is out of town and I haven't been able to obtain one

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that I am shocked to hear that your solicitor is out of town. This is precisely the kind of incompetence I was afraid of. You really must do better than this if you hope to secure Gwendolen's hand.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I refuse to be interrogated through you, Mother. I'm quite capable of speaking for myself.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I apologize for any inconvenience I may have caused, Lady Bracknell. I assure you that I am not trying to deceive you or conceal any information.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that I am astonished that you would even think to deceive me, a lady of my standing and experience, with such a flimsy excuse. Your lack of foresight and preparedness is a serious concern for a potential son-in-law.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand your concerns, Lady Bracknell, and I assure you that I am doing my best to provide the necessary documentation, despite the difficulties I am facing.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist that you produce a satisfactory explanation for your absence from your townhouse, Mr. Worthing. I will not be satisfied with vague assurances and empty promises.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I'm still trying to gather the necessary papers, Lady Bracknell. I had expected to have them by now, but the process has been... more complicated than I anticipated.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I'll have no more of this inquisition, Mother. I'll come up now and we can discuss this further in a civilized manner.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, I am shocked that you would attempt to shift the burden of responsibility onto the paperwork, Mr. Worthing. That is a grossly inadequate explanation, and I will not be placated by such feeble excuses.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, that the delay is not due to any lack of effort on my part, but rather the complexity of the documents required.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist that you provide me with the names of the clerks who are handling your case, Mr. Worthing, that I may be assured that you are not simply trying to avoid a direct answer.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I will not be lectured on the importance of paperwork, Mother. I know what I want, and I will not be swayed by your questioning.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
